newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK, Taiwan, China stocks firm despite Deng worries.
newsitem.headline: HK, Taiwan, China stocks firm despite Deng worries.

text.p: Stocks in Hong Kong, Taiwan and China moved cautiously higher on Wednesday despite lingering concern over the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

Hong Kong stocks weakened slightly after opening higher, and then bounced back, leaving the Hang Seng Index up 17.86 points, or 0.14 percent, at 13,120.80. It shed 41.68 points, or 0.32 percent on Tuesday.

"Things looked a little better early on but there is still a slight amount of continued worry about Deng," Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities said of the swings in the market's direction.
After falling sharply on Monday and Tuesday, stocks in Shanghai and Shenzhen moved higher early on Wednesday.
Traders said remarks from Beijing's foreign ministry that there had been no major change in Deng's health prompted a modest recovery.
"The foreign ministry statement helped improve sentiment a little, pushing the index up in a technical rebount this morning" one broker said.
"But concerns over Deng's health have not disappeared and room for further rises will be limited," he added.
Shenzhen's domestic A share index rose 18.61 points, or 5.51 percent to 356.26 points, while the foreign-owned B share index gained 4.82 points, or 3.50 percent, to 142.54 points.
The A share index had lost 9.76 percent on Tuesday, while the B shares shed 9.58 percent.
Shanghai's A share index was up 50.04 points, or 5.36 percent to 982.823 points after losing 8.97 percent on Tuesday.
Nikko's Rossiter said investors were beginning to shift their funds out of Hong Kong as a result of the uncertainty over Deng's health. "People are hesitant to get in now," he said.
The 92-year old leader's health stirred intense speculation among Japanese and Hong Kong media on Wednesday after the country's leaders cut short out-of-town trips.
Japan's Kyodo news agency said Deng suffered a brain haemorrhage last Friday and had been taken to hospital.
Hong Kong's Ming Pao newspaper said Deng was recuperating at home with a team of doctors attending to him.
Taiwan shares closed higher, but off early highs, as worries receded that the central bank would take measures to curb the market's recent wild gains.
Concern over Deng's health, which had hit the market on Tuesday, were not a factor on Wednesday.
The weighted index ended 14.82 points, or 0.19 percent higher, at 7,656.85.

Elsewhere in Asia, Tokyo stocks were moderately lower, dragged down by losses in construction and banking shares. The market had opened higher on institutional buying following Wall Street's nearly 80 point advance on Tuesday.
The key Nikkei 225 average fell 79.55 points, or 0.43 percent, to 18,391.20.
Trading was quiet in other Asian markets, with South Korean stocks up 1.54 points, or 0.22 percent, at 708.48, and Thai shares 6.44 points, or 0.92 percent higher, at 706.59.
The U.S. dollar was steady against the Japanese yen and German mark.
Early gains were eroded after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar's rise was the result of an overdue correction and that he hoped the correction had ended.
The dollar was quoted at 124.01/04 yen, compared with 123.82/90 in New York overnight, and at 1.6860/63 marks, compared with 1.6850/60.
